docs.title: NYC Airbnb - how much should a listing charge per night?
docs.text:
Semester project for the Artificial Neural Networks and Deep Learning course, by Gustavo Cruz, Henrique Mayor and Pedro Fardin. We use the New York City Airbnb Open Data (48,895 listings, 2019 snapshot) and the task is regression on price.

The project has a few deliverables and each one gets its own page:

deliverable status 1 Exploratory Data Analysis - data dictionary, quality, distributions, correlations and the preprocessing pipeline done 2 Regression with a neural network - baselines, MLP in PyTorch, regularisation, hyperparameter search, test evaluation over 5 seeds and error analysis done

docs.title: Running the code
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/henriquessm/nyc-airbnb-project.git
cd nyc-airbnb-project
pip install -r requirements.txt
python code/eda.py          # regenerates every figure and docs/projects/eda/results.json
python code/preprocess.py   # prints the pipeline sanity report
python code/regression.py   # trains the baselines and the network, figures + docs/projects/regression/results.json

The dataset is committed under data/ so a clean clone runs without a Kaggle account.

docs.title: EDA - New York City Airbnb Open Data
docs.text:
Team: Gustavo Cruz, Henrique Mayor and Pedro Fardin.

Task: regression. Target: price (USD per night of an Airbnb listing in NYC, 2019 snapshot).

The question we want a model to answer at the end of the semester is simple: given what a listing is and where it is, how much does it charge per night? This report is the first step. No model is trained here; the goal is to understand the data well enough to build the preprocessing pipeline that the neural network will consume.

Everything below is reproducible with two commands from a clean clone (see the README):

python code/eda.py          # figures + docs/projects/eda/results.json
python code/preprocess.py   # pipeline sanity report

All numbers quoted in the text are read from results.json, which code/eda.py writes, so the text and the code cannot drift apart silently.

docs.title: 0. Proposal
docs.text: Dataset New York City Airbnb Open Data (Kaggle, dgomonov) Size 48,895 rows × 16 columns Target price (integer, USD / night) Numerical features 7 after dropping identifiers (latitude, longitude, minimum_nights, number_of_reviews, reviews_per_month, calculated_host_listings_count, availability_365) Categorical features 3 (neighbourhood_group, neighbourhood, room_type) Motivation Price is the one number every host has to pick and every guest reacts to. The dataset is small enough to iterate fast, has a clear geographic structure and mixes clean numeric features with a 221-level categorical, which is exactly the kind of thing we want to learn to feed a neural network. First risk The target is absurdly skewed (one listing at $10,000, median $106). Whatever we do, the loss will be dominated by a handful of rows unless we model log-price.

docs.title: A. Data dictionary
docs.text:
The file is the public Airbnb snapshot for New York City compiled by Inside Airbnb and re-published on Kaggle (AB_NYC_2019.csv). Each row is one listing (one ad on the platform) as it looked in mid-2019; the most recent last_review in the file is 2019-07-08. Listings belong to hosts, and a host can own many listings.

column meaning type unit / values id listing identifier on Airbnb int - name title of the ad, written by the host free text - host_id host identifier int - host_name first name of the host text - neighbourhood_group borough categorical Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, Bronx, Staten Island neighbourhood neighbourhood inside the borough categorical 221 values latitude position float decimal degrees longitude position float decimal degrees room_type what is being rented categorical Entire home/apt, Private room, Shared room price target, nightly price set by the host int USD minimum_nights minimum length of stay the host accepts int nights number_of_reviews total reviews received int count last_review date of the most recent review date YYYY-MM-DD reviews_per_month average reviews per month since the first review float reviews / month calculated_host_listings_count how many listings the same host has in the file int count availability_365 days the calendar is open in the next 365 int days (0-365)

Two things that are not obvious from the names and that we checked: calculated_host_listings_count is exactly the number of times each host_id appears in this file (100.0% of rows match a groupby('host_id').size()), so it is derived from the file itself, not from Airbnb's full catalogue; and reviews_per_month is missing exactly on the listings with number_of_reviews == 0 (the two sets coincide for all 48,895 rows), which settles how to impute it later.

docs.title: B. Quality
docs.text:
Missing values. Only four columns have any, and two of them are the same 10,052 rows:

column missing % last_review 10,052 20.56% reviews_per_month 10,052 20.56% host_name 21 0.04% name 16 0.03%

The 20.56% are listings that never got a review, so this is not "lost" information: it is a legitimate state ("no reviews yet"). Everything else is complete.

Duplicates. 0 fully duplicated rows and 0 duplicated id. We also looked at name: 47,905 distinct titles for 48,895 rows, and the repeated ones are things like "Cozy room in Brooklyn" from different hosts, not copies of the same listing.

Impossible or inconsistent values, quantified:

  • price == 0: 11 listings. A nightly price of zero is not a price, it is a placeholder; these rows are removed from the dataset before anything else (48,895 → 48,884 rows).
  • price >= 1000: 298 listings (0.61%), maximum $10,000. They are extreme but not impossible (penthouses exist, and so do hosts who set an absurd price to block the calendar). We keep them and deal with them through the log transform of the target (section 4A).
  • minimum_nights > 365: 14 listings, maximum 1,250 nights; 747 listings (1.5%) ask for more than 30 nights. Nobody books 3.4 years on Airbnb; these are hosts using the field to effectively hide the listing. They are capped by the outlier strategy, not deleted.
  • availability_365 == 0: 17,533 listings (35.9%). This is the most interesting "suspicious" value: a third of the listings have no open date in the next year. It is not an error (the calendar is simply closed, or fully booked), but it means that availability_365 carries an "is this listing active?" signal as much as a supply signal. We keep it as is and flag it as a risk.
  • reviews_per_month > 20: 3 listings (max 58.5). Possible for a very active shared room, so left alone; the 99th-percentile clipping takes care of them anyway.
  • Coordinates: latitude in [40.4998, 40.9131], longitude in [-74.2444, -73.7130], which is inside the city. Nothing to fix.

Columns dropped and why:

column reason id, host_id identifiers; a model that learns them is memorising rows name free text, 47,905 distinct values; could feed an NLP feature later, but not in this pipeline host_name first name of the host, a quasi-identifier with no legitimate predictive meaning last_review a date that is only informative relative to the snapshot date; its "has reviews" information already lives in number_of_reviews and reviews_per_month

Leakage. No column is computed from price. The strongest rank correlation of any numeric column with the target in the raw file is longitude (Spearman -0.438), then latitude (0.136) and calculated_host_listings_count (-0.106). Nothing is suspiciously high, and the categorical columns describe the listing, not its price. We do not consider calculated_host_listings_count a leak even though it is derived from the file, because it does not use the target.

docs.title: C. Target
docs.text:
After removing the 11 zero-price rows, price looks like this (n = 48,884):

mean median std min Q1 Q3 P90 P95 P99 max skewness kurtosis $152.76 $106 $240.17 $10 $69 $175 $269 $355 $799 $10,000 19.12 585.6

The mean is 44% above the median, the standard deviation is larger than the mean, and a skewness of 19 is far beyond anything a squared-error loss can handle. Figure 1(a) shows the histogram up to $1,000 (99.51% of the rows; the remaining 0.49% are a tail that stretches 10× further to the right). Figure 1(b) shows log1p(price): skewness drops to 0.63, the shape is close to a slightly right-skewed bell, and the small spikes are hosts rounding to $50, $100, $150, $200.

Conclusion: the model will be trained on log1p(price) and predictions exponentiated back. This single decision removes most of the "outlier" problem in the target.

docs.title: D. Train and test
docs.text:
Split 80 / 20 with random_state=42, done right after the zero-price filter and before any other decision: 39,107 training rows and 9,777 test rows (20.0%). Since the task is regression we cannot stratify on the class, so we stratified on deciles of log1p(price), which guarantees the test set sees the same price range as the training set. The check in Figure 2 and the table below confirm it also preserved the categorical mix without us asking for it:

train test median price $106 $106 mean price $152.3 $154.7 Manhattan / Brooklyn / Queens / Bronx / Staten Island 44.4 / 41.1 / 11.6 / 2.2 / 0.8 % 44.0 / 41.3 / 11.7 / 2.2 / 0.8 % Entire / Private / Shared 51.9 / 45.7 / 2.4 % 52.5 / 45.3 / 2.3 %

One detail worth recording now: the neighbourhood Fort Wadsworth has a single listing in the whole file, and it fell in the test set, so the test set contains a category the training set never saw. This is exactly the case the encoder in section 4A has to survive.

From here on every statistic, figure and fitted parameter uses the training set only.

docs.title: A. Numerical features
docs.text:
Descriptive statistics of the 7 numerical features on the training set (n = 39,107; reviews_per_month has 31,051 non-missing values):

feature mean median std Q1 Q3 min max skewness % zeros latitude 40.729 40.723 0.055 40.690 40.763 40.500 40.913 0.24 0 longitude -73.952 -73.956 0.046 -73.983 -73.936 -74.243 -73.713 1.29 0 availability_365 112.7 45 131.8 0 227 0 365 0.77 36.0 minimum_nights 7.08 2 20.74 1 5 1 1,250 21.8 0 number_of_reviews 23.3 5 44.5 1 24 0 629 3.66 20.6 reviews_per_month 1.37 0.71 1.69 0.19 2.00 0.01 58.5 3.35 0 calculated_host_listings_count 7.24 1 33.3 1 2 1 327 7.85 0

The table already tells the story, so we spent the two figures of this item on the shapes that matter for preprocessing. Figure 3 shows all seven distributions, with the four heavy-tailed counts on a log1p axis (on a linear axis they are a single bar at zero):

  • latitude and longitude are roughly bell-shaped with a few bumps (the boroughs). They are the only two features that can be standardised as they are.
  • minimum_nights, number_of_reviews, reviews_per_month and calculated_host_listings_count are all extremely right-skewed (skewness 3.3 to 21.8) and, even on a log scale, still skewed. 20.6% of the listings have zero reviews; the median host has exactly 1 listing but the maximum has 327.
  • availability_365 is not skewed in the usual sense but it is bimodal at the edges.

Figure 4 zooms in on the two spikes we think a model needs to know about:

  • (a) 66.4% of the listings ask for 1 to 3 nights (10,228 / 9,343 / 6,390 listings), but there is an isolated spike at 30 nights with 2,993 listings (7.7%), bigger than any value between 8 and 29. This is New York's rule that forbids short stays in many buildings: those are long-term rentals disguised as Airbnbs, and they will behave differently in price.
  • (b) 36.0% of the training listings have 0 available days, and another 2.7% have all 365. The spike at zero is 15,000 rows, the next bin is below 1,000.

Conclusion: two scales (coordinates vs counts), four features that need a log, and two features with spikes that a scaler will not remove but that a network can learn from if we do not destroy them.

docs.title: B. Categorical features
docs.text:
feature cardinality (train) most frequent % least frequent n categories below 1% neighbourhood_group 5 Manhattan 44.4% Staten Island 295 1 room_type 3 Entire home/apt 51.9% Shared room 938 0 neighbourhood 220 (221 in the full file) Williamsburg 8.0% Richmondtown and 8 others 1 195

Figure 5 crosses the two small categoricals. Manhattan (17,359) and Brooklyn (16,060) hold 85.5% of the listings between them; Queens has 4,522, the Bronx 871 and Staten Island only 295. Entire homes dominate in Manhattan (10,570 vs 6,404 private rooms), private rooms dominate in Brooklyn (8,148 vs 7,582) and in every other borough. Shared rooms are rare everywhere: 938 listings in total (2.4%) and only 8 in Staten Island, so any per-cell statistic involving them has to be read with care.

neighbourhood is the high-cardinality problem of this dataset. Figure 6 shows the 25 largest of the 220 neighbourhoods; they already hold 71.1% of the training listings, and the top 10 alone hold 47.9%. At the other end, 112 neighbourhoods have fewer than 30 training listings, 9 have exactly one, and together the 112 rare ones account for only 1,089 rows (2.78%). One-hot encoding all 220 would create 112 columns that are almost always zero and that the test set may contradict (Fort Wadsworth). That is the finding behind the rare-category grouping in section 4A.

Conclusion: room_type and neighbourhood_group can be one-hot encoded as they are; neighbourhood needs a frequency threshold, and Shared room / Staten Island / Bronx are small enough that the model will have few examples to learn from.

docs.title: A. Numerical × numerical
docs.text:
We used Spearman rather than Pearson. Section 2A showed that five of the eight numerical columns (including the target) have skewness above 3 and maxima hundreds of times the median; Pearson is a linear correlation and a single $10,000 listing or a 1,250-night minimum moves it arbitrarily. Spearman works on ranks, which is also the right notion of "related" for features that will be log-transformed anyway. The difference is not academic: for longitude × price Pearson gives -0.15 and Spearman gives -0.44.

Reading Figure 7, the pairs that stand out:

pair Spearman Pearson number_of_reviews × reviews_per_month 0.71 0.55 longitude × price -0.44 -0.15 availability_365 × calculated_host_listings_count 0.41 0.23 availability_365 × reviews_per_month 0.39 0.18 minimum_nights × reviews_per_month -0.29 -0.13

Everything else is below 0.25 in absolute value. With the target, the only feature with a correlation worth the name is longitude (-0.44, i.e. prices go up as you go west, towards Manhattan); latitude is 0.13, calculated_host_listings_count -0.11, minimum_nights 0.10 and the rest is below 0.1. No single numeric feature predicts price on its own; the signal is in the interaction between position and room type, which is what the next two sections show.

Figure 8(a) is the one redundant pair: reviews_per_month is number_of_reviews divided by the months since the first review, so the two are the same information at two time scales. We keep both for now (the ratio adds "recency", a 2-review listing from 2012 and one from last month are different), but if the network overfits this is the first pair to prune. Figure 8(b) shows that the 0.41 between availability and host portfolio size is not noise: hosts with dozens of listings keep their calendars open all year (the horizontal bands at the top sit at 300+ days), while single-listing hosts spread across the whole range.

Figure 9 explains the -0.44 with longitude: the price is a function of distance to Manhattan, not of longitude itself. The bright band is Manhattan below Central Park plus the waterfront of Brooklyn; everything east of -73.9 is cheap no matter the latitude. Conclusion: latitude and longitude have to enter the model together (a network can learn the 2-D shape, a linear model on each coordinate cannot), and neither should be dropped.

docs.title: B. Categorical × target
docs.text:
Figure 10 shows the price distribution for each borough × room type cell, on a log scale. Medians:

borough Entire home/apt Private room Shared room all Manhattan $190 $90 $69 $150 Brooklyn $149 $65 $35 $90 Queens $120 $59 $37 $75 Bronx $100 $55 $38 $65 Staten Island $101.5 $55 $52.5 $75 all $160 $70 $45 $106

Two readings. First, room_type is the strongest single predictor in the dataset: entire homes cost 2.3× a private room and 3.6× a shared room at the median, and the boxes barely overlap inside each borough. Second, the borough effect is a roughly constant multiplier on top of room type (Manhattan ≈ 1.3-1.4× Brooklyn in every room type), which is good news for a log target because a multiplier becomes an additive offset. Just these two categoricals, used as group means, explain 45.4% of the variance of log1p(price) on the training set.

Conclusion of Figure 10: room type first, borough second, and the two combine multiplicatively, so a log target plus one-hot encoding of both is the right representation.

Figure 11 goes one level down, to neighbourhoods with at least 30 training listings (108 of them). The spread is 7.5× between the most expensive (Tribeca, median $299.5, then NoHo $249.5 and Flatiron $225) and the cheapest (Corona $40, Borough Park $51, Woodhaven $51.5). The top 12 are all Manhattan south of Central Park except DUMBO; the bottom 12 are Queens, the Bronx and outer Brooklyn. Replacing borough by neighbourhood in the group-mean experiment above raises the explained variance from 45.4% to 53.7%.

Conclusion of Figure 11: neighbourhood adds about 8 points of explained variance on top of borough, which is enough to justify keeping it despite the cardinality, but the gain comes from the ~100 neighbourhoods with enough data, not from the 112 rare ones.

docs.title: C. Numerical × categorical
docs.text:
Figure 12(a), availability_365 by room type: the medians are 42, 45 and 90 days for entire home, private and shared rooms, and the third quartile jumps from 229 and 215 to 342. Shared rooms differ in both location and spread: they are open more of the year and much more variable. They are also the cell with the fewest closed calendars (25.9% at zero vs 35.2% and 37.5%). Figure 12(b), minimum_nights: medians 3 / 2 / 1 nights, Q3 at 5 / 4 / 3. The groups differ in location (entire homes ask for longer stays) but the spread on the log scale is similar, and the outliers above 30 nights exist in all three.

Figure 13(a), number_of_reviews by borough: the median rises as we leave Manhattan (4 → 6 → 7 → 9 → 11 reviews from Manhattan to Staten Island) and so does Q3 (19 → 25 → 33 → 31.5 → 39.5). A difference in location and spread in the same direction: outer-borough listings are fewer but, relative to their number, more reviewed, which fits a "fewer, more committed hosts" story. Figure 13(b), calculated_host_listings_count by room type: the median is 1 for entire homes and private rooms and 2 for shared rooms; 61.1% of shared rooms belong to a host with more than one listing against 25.1% of entire homes. Here the difference is mostly spread: shared rooms are the professional-host segment.

Conclusion: the numerical features do not just shift between categories, the shared-room segment has a different variance structure (open calendars, multi-listing hosts), which is one more argument for a model that can learn interactions rather than additive effects.

docs.title: 4. Preprocessing
docs.text: Every choice below points to the finding that motivates it. The destination is a neural network, which changes two things compared with a tree model: scale matters (inputs should be roughly centred and of unit variance for the optimiser), and heavy tails matter (a few inputs at 50 standard deviations saturate the first layer).

docs.title: A. Strategies
docs.text:
Row filter (before the split). The 11 rows with price == 0 were removed (section 1B). Nothing else is deleted: 48,884 rows go into the split.

Missing values. The only real missingness is reviews_per_month (20.6% of the training set), and section 1A showed it is missing exactly when number_of_reviews == 0. The honest value is therefore 0 reviews per month, not the median; we impute with a constant 0. last_review is dropped, name and host_name are dropped, so no other column needs imputation. Still, every branch of the pipeline has a SimpleImputer in front (median for numeric, most-frequent for categorical) so that a future file with a hole in latitude does not crash a model in production.

Outliers. Motivated by Table 2A and Figure 3: minimum_nights (max 1,250, skew 21.8), number_of_reviews (max 629), reviews_per_month (max 58.5) and calculated_host_listings_count (max 327, skew 7.85). The strategy is clip to the 1st-99th percentile learned on the training set, then log1p. The bounds the pipeline learned are:

feature lower upper training rows clipped minimum_nights 1 46.9 392 number_of_reviews 0 213.9 392 reviews_per_month 0 6.86 392 calculated_host_listings_count 1 232 267

In total 1,387 training rows (3.55%) had at least one value clipped (312 in the test set, using the training bounds). The 392 are not a coincidence: clipping at the 99th percentile touches about 1% of 39,107 rows per column by construction. availability_365 is bounded in [0, 365] and latitude/longitude are inside the city, so they are not clipped. The target is not clipped either: the log1p transform (section 1C, skewness 19.1 → 0.63) is what handles the $10,000 listing, and we want the model to see that such listings exist.

Figure 14 shows the four heavy-tailed features before and after the clip + log + standardise branch. Skewness goes from 21.8 → 1.3, 3.7 → 0.3, 3.5 → 0.9 and 7.8 → 3.2. calculated_host_listings_count stays skewed because 65% of the listings sit at exactly 1; no monotone transform can spread a point mass, and that is fine.

Categorical encoding. neighbourhood_group (5) and room_type (3) are one-hot encoded with handle_unknown="ignore": an unseen borough would become an all-zero row instead of an error. neighbourhood (220 in train, Figure 6) is one-hot encoded with min_frequency=30: the 112 neighbourhoods with fewer than 30 training listings are merged into one infrequent column, and handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist" sends any category never seen in training to that same column. That is how Fort Wadsworth, which only exists in the test set, is handled without special code: it lands in infrequent together with 305 other test rows. The result is 108 + 1 = 109 neighbourhood columns instead of 220. We chose one-hot over target encoding on purpose: target encoding would need to be fitted inside cross-validation to avoid leaking the target, and 109 sparse inputs are not a problem for a network.

Scaling. Coordinates range over 0.4 degrees, counts over hundreds, dummies over {0, 1}: every numeric branch ends with a StandardScaler fitted on train, so that the network sees inputs of comparable magnitude. The log comes before the scaler (standardising a skew-21 variable just rescales the outliers).

Target. log1p(price), exposed as transform_target() in the module. The pipeline itself only touches X.

docs.title: B. Dimensionality reduction
docs.text:
All three projections use the same 15 features: the 7 standardised numerical features plus the 8 dummies of neighbourhood_group and room_type, taken from the output of the fitted pipeline on the training set. The 109 neighbourhood dummies were left out on purpose: they are 98% zeros and would add 109 near-zero-variance directions that tell PCA nothing. Points are coloured by log1p(price).

PCA.

PC1 explains 25.0% and PC2 19.9%, so PC1 + PC2 = 44.9% of the variance; it takes 5 components to reach 80% and 8 to reach 95% (Figure 15a). On the 7 numerical features alone PC1 + PC2 would be 51.7%, the dummies spread the variance a bit. The loadings in Figure 16 say what the axes are:

  • PC1 is a review activity axis: reviews_per_month (0.61) and number_of_reviews (0.59) pull one way, minimum_nights (-0.40) and calculated_host_listings_count (-0.20) the other. High PC1 = short-stay listing with lots of recent reviews; low PC1 = long-minimum, multi-listing host with few reviews.
  • PC2 is a professional host axis: availability_365 (0.62), calculated_host_listings_count (0.61) and minimum_nights (0.39), all positive. It is the 0.41 correlation of Figure 8(b) turned into a direction.
  • PC3 is pure geography: latitude (0.87), with Manhattan (+0.28) against Brooklyn (-0.34).

The room-type dummies have loadings below 0.05 on every one of the first three components, which is the honest reading of Figure 15(b): the best linear 2-D picture of the features is about how the listing is operated, not about what it is, and that is why price barely shows a gradient (Spearman of PC1 with log-price is -0.15, of PC2 it is 0.07). The yellow points (expensive) are smeared through the cloud.

t-SNE (5,000 training rows sampled with seed 42, init="pca", perplexity 30 and 100):

UMAP (the same 5,000 rows, n_neighbors 15 and 100, min_dist=0.1):

Comparison. The nonlinear projections show something PCA cannot: both of them split the data into a handful of islands, and the islands are the room type × borough cells (dummies are discrete, so the neighbourhood graph that t-SNE and UMAP build is almost disconnected between cells). Inside each island there is a visible price gradient, from a dark (cheap) end to a bright (expensive) end: the "entire home in Manhattan" island is mostly green/yellow, the private-room islands are mostly purple/blue. So the structure that a model has to learn is categorical cell first, then a continuous gradient inside the cell, which PCA flattens into one cloud because the dummies carry little variance.

The parameter sweep behaves as expected. At perplexity 30 t-SNE breaks the cells into many small blobs; at 100 it merges them into 4-5 large regions with a cleaner colour gradient. UMAP with n_neighbors=15 gives sharply separated islands, with 100 the islands get bridges and the global layout is more stable. We remind ourselves that in both methods the size of an island and the distance between islands have no meaning: the shared-room island is not "far" from the others in any measurable sense, and UMAP's tighter clusters do not mean better separation than t-SNE's. The useful reading is only which points are neighbours, and that reading is consistent across the four panels.

docs.title: C. Pipeline
docs.text:
The pipeline lives in code/preprocess.py and is importable:

from code.preprocess import load_data, split_data, build_preprocessor, transform_target

df = load_data()                                  # csv + price > 0 filter
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = split_data(df) # 80/20, seed 42, stratified on log-price deciles
pre = build_preprocessor()                        # ColumnTransformer
X_train_t = pre.fit_transform(X_train)            # fit on train only
X_test_t = pre.transform(X_test)                  # test is only transformed

The ColumnTransformer has five branches, one per feature group, and python code/preprocess.py prints the sanity report:

rows after filters      : 48884
train / test rows       : 39107 / 9777
NaN in train after pipe : 0
NaN in test after pipe  : 0
X_train_t shape         : (39107, 124)
X_test_t shape          : (9777, 124)
n features out          : 124

No NaN is left in either set. The 124 output features are: 2 geo (geo__latitude, geo__longitude), 1 bounded (bounded__availability_365), 4 heavy-tailed (heavy__minimum_nights, heavy__number_of_reviews, heavy__reviews_per_month, heavy__calculated_host_listings_count), 5 borough dummies (cat__neighbourhood_group_*), 3 room-type dummies (cat__room_type_*), and 109 neighbourhood dummies (hood__neighbourhood_*, the last one being hood__neighbourhood_infrequent_sklearn). The full list is what pre.get_feature_names_out() returns and is printed by the script.

docs.title: 5. Synthesis
docs.text:
Written for whoever builds the model next.

Main findings

  1. Model log-price, not price. Skewness 19.1 on the raw target vs 0.63 after log1p (Figure 1, Table 1C). A squared-error loss on raw price would be fitting the 298 listings above $1,000.
  2. Room type and location explain half of the variance before any modelling. Group means of log-price by borough × room type give an R² of 0.454 on the training set, neighbourhood × room type gives 0.537 (Figures 10 and 11). A model that does not beat ~0.54 R² on the training set has learned nothing from the numerical features.
  3. Price is geographic in 2-D. longitude alone has Spearman -0.44 with price but the map (Figure 9) shows a "distance to lower Manhattan" shape that needs both coordinates together.
  4. The numerical features describe how a listing is operated, not what it costs. PCA's first two axes (review activity, professional host; Figure 16) carry 44.9% of the feature variance and almost no price gradient. t-SNE and UMAP (Figures 17-18) show the price gradient inside each room type × borough island.
  5. Two spikes worth a feature each: 7.7% of listings at exactly 30 minimum nights (Figure 4a) and 36.0% with zero availability (Figure 4b). The pipeline keeps the information (clipping does not touch 30, and 0 stays 0) but the modelling step could add explicit is_30_nights and is_closed flags.
  6. One redundant pair: number_of_reviews × reviews_per_month, Spearman 0.71 (Figure 8a). Kept for now, first candidate to drop.

Risks and handling plan

risk evidence plan Extreme prices dominate the loss max $10,000, kurtosis 585.6 (1C) train on log1p(price); report MAE in dollars on the test set too, so the metric is readable 36% of listings with closed calendars may be inactive, with stale prices Figure 4b keep them (no ground truth to remove them) but evaluate the error separately on availability_365 == 0 vs > 0 Rare categories: Shared room (2.4%), Staten Island (0.8%), 112 neighbourhoods with < 30 listings Tables 2B rare neighbourhoods grouped into infrequent; monitor per-borough and per-room-type error; consider embedding neighbourhood instead of one-hot if the 109 columns overfit Unseen category at test time (Fort Wadsworth) 1D handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist" already routes it to infrequent; no code change needed Collinear review features Spearman 0.71 (3A) dropout / weight decay in the network; drop reviews_per_month if validation says so Hosts with many listings share the same price policy, so rows are not independent 327 listings from one host (1B) a grouped split by host_id would be stricter; we kept the random split because the course asks for a plain stratified split, but this is the first thing to try if test error looks optimistic

Results summary

# Results summary Value 1 Dataset, task and target NYC Airbnb Open Data 2019 (Kaggle) · regression · price (USD / night) 2 Instances × features (numerical / categorical) 48,895 × 16 in the file; 48,884 × 10 features used (7 numerical / 3 categorical) + target 3 Column with the most missing values and its percentage last_review and reviews_per_month, 10,052 rows each (20.56%) 4 Dropped columns and the reason id, host_id (identifiers), name, host_name (free text / quasi-identifier), last_review (date, redundant with review counts); 11 rows with price == 0 removed 5 Mean and median of the target mean $152.76 · median $106 (skewness 19.12; 0.63 after log1p) 6 Size of the training and test sets 39,107 train · 9,777 test (80/20, seed 42, stratified on log-price deciles) 7 Most correlated numerical pair and its value number_of_reviews × reviews_per_month, Spearman 0.706 8 Rows affected by the outlier strategy 1,387 training rows (3.55%) clipped at the 1st/99th percentile in at least one of 4 features; 312 test rows 9 Variance explained by PC1 + PC2 44.9% (25.0% + 19.9%) on the 15 scaled pipeline features 10 shape of train and test after the pipeline (39,107, 124) and (9,777, 124), 0 NaN

docs.title: Regression - NYC Airbnb price with a neural network
docs.text:
Team: Gustavo Cruz, Henrique Mayor and Pedro Fardin.

Task: regression. Target: price (USD per night). Main metric: MAE in dollars on the test set.

This is the second delivery of the project. The EDA built the preprocessing pipeline; here we train a multilayer perceptron on top of it and ask two questions: does the network learn something that simpler models do not, and how far can the number it reports be trusted?

Everything below comes out of one script, from a clean clone:

pip install -r requirements.txt
python code/regression.py    # ~6 min on a GPU, CPU works too (slower)

The script writes every figure to figures/ and every number quoted here to results.json. The network and its training loop are in code/model.py, the experiment in code/regression.py. Seeds are fixed everywhere (random_state=42 for the split, seeds 42 to 46 for the networks), and the seed is set before the network is built, so it fixes the initial weights as well as the batch order.

docs.title: 0. Starting point
docs.text:
Data and split. Same file, same row filter (the 11 listings with price == 0 removed) and the same 80/20 split as the EDA, seed 42, stratified on deciles of log1p(price): 39,107 training rows and 9,777 test rows. The validation set comes out of the training set: 15% of it, with the same seed and the same stratification, so the three sets have the same price range (median $106 in all three).

set rows used for train 33,240 fitting the pipeline and every model validation 5,867 early stopping, every choice of model and hyperparameter test 9,777 section 5 only, once, after everything was frozen

Pipeline. The ColumnTransformer from code/preprocess.py is imported as is and fitted on the 33,240 training rows only; validation and test are only transformed. Because it is fitted on fewer rows than in the EDA, five fewer neighbourhoods reach the 30-listing threshold, so the output has 119 features instead of 124 (104 neighbourhood columns, the last one being the infrequent bucket; 3.1% of the validation rows fall in it). Nothing else changed. The model is trained on log1p(price) (transform_target(), EDA section 1C: skewness 19.1 on the raw price, 0.63 on the log) and every prediction is brought back with expm1 before any metric is computed, so all metrics are in dollars.

Main metric: MAE in USD on the test set. The target has a tail that no metric can ignore (kurtosis 585.6, one listing at $10,000). RMSE squares the errors and would be decided by the 62 test listings above $1,000; MAE treats a $50 error as a $50 error wherever it happens and is the number a host understands. It also matches the way we train: a model fitted on the log predicts something close to the conditional median of the price, and the median is what minimises the absolute error. RMSE, R² and MedAE are reported next to it.

Success criterion, written before training any network:

The network's test MAE (mean over 5 seeds) is at least 10% lower than the MAE of the best of the trivial and linear baselines, and the gap is larger than the variation between seeds.

Why 10% and not more: the EDA found that group means of log-price by room type × neighbourhood already explain 53.7% of its variance on the training set. A linear model with one-hot room type and neighbourhood captures most of that for free; what is left for the network is the 2-D shape of the map (EDA Figure 9) and the interactions between room type, location and how the listing is operated (EDA section 3C). A 10% cut in MAE on top of a linear model is what we expected those interactions to be worth.

docs.title: 1. Baselines
docs.text:
All baselines use the same pipeline output (119 features) and the same log target, are fitted on train and evaluated on validation:

  • Trivial: DummyRegressor(strategy="mean") on log1p(price), which predicts the constant $113.12 for every listing, and DummyRegressor(strategy="median") on the price in dollars, which predicts $106.
  • Linear: Ridge, with alpha chosen on validation among 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10 and 100. The MAE is $61.00 to $61.02 for every alpha up to 10 and $61.13 at 100: with 33,240 rows for 119 features the penalty barely matters. alpha = 10 was kept.
  • Optional: HistGradientBoostingRegressor with default settings (random_state=42), as a nonlinear reference.
model (validation) MAE ($) RMSE ($) R² MedAE ($) R² on log-price Dummy, mean of log (constant $113.12) 85.96 240.07 -0.031 48.12 0.000 Dummy, median (constant $106) 85.80 241.40 -0.042 46.00 -0.009 Ridge (alpha=10) 61.00 221.40 0.124 25.74 0.564 Gradient boosting 58.11 217.61 0.153 24.05 0.612

Reading the table:

  • Ridge removes 29% of the error of the trivial model ($85.80 → $61.00). This is the best of the two required baselines, so it is the reference for the criterion of step 0.
  • R² in dollars is low for every model (0.12 for Ridge) while R² on the log scale is 0.56. Both are correct: the dollar R² is dominated by the squared errors on the few listings at several thousand dollars, which no model gets right (section 6). The log R² of Ridge (0.564) is close to the 0.537 of the group means in the EDA, which is what a linear model on one-hot categories should give.
  • Gradient boosting is already $2.89 better than Ridge. Trees capture interactions without being told, so this gap is a first measure of the nonlinear structure available, and a realistic target for the network.

docs.title: 2. The network
docs.text:
The network is a plain MLP in PyTorch (code/model.py, class MLP):

input (119) -> Linear 256 -> ReLU -> [Dropout] -> Linear 128 -> ReLU -> [Dropout] -> Linear 1

The base configuration is two hidden layers of 256 and 128 units, no regularisation; the version that went to the test set adds dropout 0.2 (section 4). Every choice:

  • Two hidden layers. One hidden layer is enough in theory (universal approximation), but the theorem says nothing about how many units it takes. The EDA showed a structure in two levels: a categorical cell first (room type × borough), then a continuous gradient inside the cell (EDA Figures 17-18). Two layers let the first build features such as "entire home in lower Manhattan" and the second combine them. A third layer was tried in the search (section 4) and did not help.
  • Widths 256 → 128. The first layer is wider than the input (119) so that it has room for combinations of inputs, then the width halves towards the single output. The search also tried 128 → 64 and 512 → 256.
  • ReLU. Its derivative is exactly 1 where the unit is active, so the gradient is not shrunk on the way back (a sigmoid shrinks it by at least 4 per layer), and it is the default for MLPs on tabular data.
  • He (Kaiming) initialisation for the hidden layers, biases at zero. The variance of the activations is multiplied at each layer by n·σ²·ρ, with n the fan-in and ρ = 1/2 for ReLU (it zeroes half of the inputs); He sets σ² = 2/n so the factor is 1. PyTorch's default for nn.Linear has variance 1/(3n), a sixth of that. With two layers either would train, but He is the one made for ReLU.
  • Output: 1 linear unit, no activation, because log-price is an unbounded real number. Its bias starts at the mean of the training log-price (4.737, i.e. $113): the network starts exactly at the trivial baseline instead of spending the first epochs learning the offset.
  • Loss: Huber with δ = 1 on log1p(price) (nn.HuberLoss(delta=1.0)). The EDA found prices that are not real prices: $10,000 listings, "blocking" prices on closed calendars. On the log scale most residuals are within ±1 (a factor of e ≈ 2.7 on the price; Figure 3c), and there Huber is the squared error. Beyond 1 it grows linearly, so a $9,999 listing predicted at $117 (a log residual of 4.4) pulls the weights like a residual of 4.4, not like 4.4² = 19. MSE on the log would let a few placeholder prices steer the fit; MAE would be robust but has a constant gradient that does not shrink near the optimum.

Number of parameters.

layer computation parameters hidden 1 119 × 256 + 256 30,720 hidden 2 256 × 128 + 128 32,896 output 128 × 1 + 1 129 total 63,745

That is 1.92 parameters per training row (63,745 / 33,240). The network has more than enough capacity to memorise noise, and Figure 1(b) shows that it does if nobody stops it. This is why early stopping (section 3) is not optional, and why section 4 tries to regularise it.

docs.title: 3. Training
docs.text:
setting value reason optimizer AdamW Adam is the course's starting point for an MLP on tabular data: one learning rate works for all layers because each parameter's step is rescaled by the running size of its gradients. AdamW is Adam with the weight decay applied directly to the weights instead of through the gradient, which matters in section 4. Biases and normalisation gains are not decayed. learning rate 1e-3 Adam's usual default. The search (section 4) tried 3e-4 and 3e-3: 3e-3 stops at epoch 6 with a worse MAE ($59.14 vs $58.50 for the same network), 3e-4 needs 71 epochs to get to the same place. batch 256 Inside the usual 32-512 range: 130 updates per epoch, a gradient estimate with noise ∝ 1/√B that is neither too noisy nor too smooth, and fast on the GPU. epochs up to 300, patience 20 Validation loss is evaluated after every epoch; training stops when it has not improved for 20 epochs and the best weights are restored. The validation curve has bumps that last 3-4 epochs (Figure 1a), so a patience of 20 does not stop on noise.

The loop (train() in code/model.py) is the course's skeleton: train on shuffled mini-batches, switch to model.eval() and compute the validation loss under torch.no_grad(), keep a copy of the state_dict whenever it improves, stop after patience epochs without improvement and load the best copy back. The copy is kept in memory instead of best.pt on disk, which is the same thing. Both curves are computed in eval mode on the whole set at the end of each epoch, so dropout does not make the training curve look worse than it is.

Reading Figure 1. The validation loss starts at 0.0933 at epoch 1, already close to its best, because the output bias starts at the mean and Adam moves fast. It reaches its minimum of 0.0895 at epoch 13; the training loss at that point is 0.078. After that the two curves separate: the training loss keeps falling (0.069 when early stopping fires at epoch 33) while the validation loss drifts up to 0.096. Overfitting starts around epoch 13. Panel (b) is the same network left for 120 epochs without early stopping: training loss 0.047, validation loss 0.109 at the end, the textbook shape of a model memorising the training set. It converges, quickly, and then it overfits; early stopping gives back the epoch-13 weights.

docs.title: Techniques compared
docs.text:
Four variants of the base network, same seed, same everything else, compared with the network without any regularisation. All numbers on validation, at the best epoch:

variant val MAE ($) val loss best epoch gap (val - train loss) none 58.50 0.0895 13 0.0115 weight decay 0.05 (AdamW) 58.54 0.0894 13 0.0110 dropout 0.2 58.03 0.0890 42 0.0142 BatchNorm 58.95 0.0900 6 0.0081 dropout 0.2 + weight decay 0.05 58.12 0.0890 42 0.0141

  • Dropout 0.2 (each hidden unit switched off with probability 0.2 during training, the survivors scaled by 1/0.8, nothing switched off at evaluation) is the only technique that improves validation: $58.03 vs $58.50. Figure 2(b) shows why: the generalisation gap grows about half as fast per epoch (0.006 at epoch 13 against 0.0115 without it), so the network can train for 42 epochs instead of 13 before validation turns. The gap at the best epoch is larger only because it is reached much later.
  • Weight decay 0.05 changes almost nothing. With AdamW each step multiplies the weights by (1 - lr·λ) = (1 - 5·10⁻⁵); over the ~1,700 steps before early stopping that is a shrinkage of about 8%. Early stopping already limits how far the weights travel, so the extra penalty arrives too late to matter. Added to dropout it does not help either ($58.12).
  • BatchNorm after each hidden linear layer (before the ReLU, dropout would go after it) converges fastest (best epoch 6) and has the smallest gap, but the worst MAE ($58.95). Our inputs are already standardised by the pipeline, so there is little scale to fix, and the noise BatchNorm injects through the batch statistics did not translate into a better fit here.

The differences are small: all five variants are within $0.92 of each other. The table says dropout is the one worth keeping; it does not say regularisation transforms this model.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
The grid has 216 combinations: hidden layers (128, 64), (256, 128), (512, 256) or (256, 256, 128); learning rate 3e-4, 1e-3 or 3e-3; weight decay 0, 0.01 or 0.1; dropout 0, 0.1 or 0.3; BatchNorm or not. We sampled 12 of them at random (seed 42), added the base network and the four variants above, and trained all 17 configurations with early stopping, batch 256. The rule, fixed before running it, is the lowest validation MAE. Sorted:

# configuration params best epoch val MAE ($) val RMSE ($) val MedAE ($) 1 [256×128] lr 1e-3, dropout 0.2 63,745 42 58.03 219.06 23.19 2 [256×128] lr 1e-3, dropout 0.2, wd 0.05 63,745 42 58.12 218.95 23.09 3 [256×256×128] lr 1e-3 129,537 13 58.21 219.90 23.20 4 [512×256] lr 1e-3, wd 0.01, dropout 0.1, BN 194,561 21 58.32 219.42 23.36 5 [512×256] lr 3e-3, dropout 0.1, BN 194,561 21 58.35 219.34 23.75 6 [128×64] lr 1e-3, dropout 0.1 23,681 55 58.43 218.01 23.74 7 [128×64] lr 3e-3, wd 0.01 23,681 13 58.50 219.13 23.77 8 [256×128] lr 1e-3 (base) 63,745 13 58.50 219.11 23.26 9 [256×256×128] lr 3e-3, wd 0.1, dropout 0.3, BN 130,817 54 58.51 219.86 24.09 10 [256×128] lr 1e-3, wd 0.05 63,745 13 58.54 219.07 23.23 11 [512×256] lr 3e-4, dropout 0.3, BN 194,561 71 58.56 218.77 24.09 12 [256×128] lr 3e-3, BN 64,513 13 58.64 219.67 24.24 13 [512×256] lr 3e-3, wd 0.1, dropout 0.1, BN 194,561 26 58.95 217.52 24.62 14 [256×128] lr 1e-3, BN 64,513 6 58.95 218.87 24.32 15 [128×64] lr 1e-3 23,681 17 59.07 218.22 24.42 16 [256×128] lr 3e-3 63,745 6 59.14 218.08 25.01 17 [256×256×128] lr 3e-3, wd 0.1 129,537 6 59.41 217.02 25.08

Chosen: [256×128], ReLU, dropout 0.2, AdamW lr 1e-3, no weight decay, batch 256. Patterns in the table: dropout appears in 5 of the top 6; the three runs that stopped at epoch 6 (lr 3e-3, or BatchNorm, without dropout) are among the bottom four; size matters little, every width from 23,681 to 194,561 parameters appears both in the top half and in the bottom half.

How much the ranking can be trusted. The whole table spans $1.38, and the top 8 are within $0.47. Section 5 retrains the chosen configuration with 5 seeds: its validation MAE varies from $58.03 to $58.53 (standard deviation $0.19) just by changing the seed. The configuration we chose was evaluated on its luckiest seed (the mean over the 5 seeds is $58.34), which is the selection optimism the course warns about: pick the best of 17 noisy numbers and the winner is partly the noise. The top 3 or 4 configurations are statistically the same model; we report the one the rule picked and do not claim it is better than the runners-up.

docs.title: 5. Test evaluation
docs.text:
The chosen configuration was trained again from scratch with 5 seeds (42 to 46), each with early stopping on the same validation set, and each evaluated once on the test set. The baselines were fitted in section 1 and are evaluated on the same test rows; gradient boosting was also run with the same 5 seeds. Nothing in sections 1-4 was chosen with the test set, and the test set was not used to change anything afterwards.

model (test, 9,777 rows) MAE ($) RMSE ($) R² MedAE ($) MAPE (%) R² on log-price Dummy, mean of log 86.06 267.74 -0.025 48.12 60.94 0.000 Dummy, median 85.93 268.94 -0.034 46.00 56.99 -0.009 Ridge 62.18 252.34 0.090 26.27 34.45 0.550 Gradient boosting (5 seeds) 58.71 ± 0.08 246.87 ± 0.52 0.129 ± 0.004 23.97 ± 0.09 32.21 ± 0.10 0.603 ± 0.001 MLP, chosen (5 seeds) 59.10 ± 0.23 248.47 ± 1.10 0.118 ± 0.008 23.59 ± 0.09 31.83 ± 0.27 0.589 ± 0.002

Per seed, the network's test MAE is $58.80, $59.42, $59.15, $59.14 and $59.01, with early stopping at epochs 42, 20, 39, 40 and 33. MAPE is reported because the price never gets close to zero (the minimum is $10).

Figure 3. (a) On log axes the cloud follows the diagonal from $30 to about $300 and then flattens: the network predicts more than $600 for only 11 test listings while 166 cost more than that, so the expensive end is underestimated, some listings by thousands of dollars. (b) In dollars the residuals fan out as the prediction grows (a $200 listing can be off by $200, a \(50 one cannot), and the parallel diagonal stripes are the round prices hosts choose (\)100, $150, \(200) minus a smooth prediction; 85 points fall beyond ±\)600. (c) On the log scale, the scale the network was trained on, the residuals are centred on zero with a roughly constant spread, plus a handful of points 3 to 4.4 above the line: the listings priced at several thousand dollars.

Was the criterion met? No. The network's test MAE is 4.95% lower than Ridge's ($59.10 vs $62.18); the criterion asked for 10% (a MAE of $55.96 or less).

Is the gap larger than the variation between seeds? Against Ridge, yes: the gap is $3.08 and the network's standard deviation over seeds is \(0.23, so the gap is **13.6 standard deviations**, and the worst seed (\)59.42) is still $2.76 better than Ridge. The network is reliably better than the linear model, just not by as much as we hoped. Against gradient boosting, no: boosting is $0.40 better on average, about 1.7 of the network's standard deviations, and its spread is smaller. On this table, the network and boosting tie, with a slight edge to boosting, which trains in a few seconds with default settings. The network is slightly better on MedAE and MAPE (the typical listing) and slightly worse on MAE, RMSE and R² (the tail).

Why RMSE and R² look so bad. RMSE/MAE = 248.5/59.1 = 4.2, against about 1.25 for Gaussian errors: a few huge misses. The 1% largest errors (97 listings) account for 27.2% of the total absolute error, and the 62 test listings above $1,000 are enough to keep R² in dollars near 0.12 for every model. Without those 62 listings the network's MAE is $45.45 (RMSE $85.37) against $48.56 for Ridge. On the log scale, R² is 0.589 for the network against 0.550 for Ridge.

docs.title: 6. Error analysis
docs.text:
All numbers in this section use the seed-42 network on the test set (MAE $58.80). Nothing here was used to choose or change the model. "Bias" is the mean of prediction minus actual: negative means the network underestimates.

group n MAE ($) MedAE ($) bias ($) median price ($) MAE / median price Entire home/apt 5,129 84.32 38.94 -41.42 160 53% Private room 4,428 30.88 14.72 -11.14 70 44% Shared room 220 25.78 10.36 -7.67 49 53% Manhattan 4,301 82.35 32.01 -43.88 150 55% Brooklyn 4,035 43.25 19.75 -16.01 91 48% Queens 1,144 32.19 16.99 -7.06 75 43% Bronx 219 28.71 14.83 -6.75 65 44% Staten Island 78 39.17 20.59 -7.48 67 58% price < $50 1,003 20.02 16.73 +19.56 40 50% $50-100 3,371 20.72 13.81 +12.94 70 30% $100-200 3,461 34.41 27.15 +5.30 139 25% $200-500 1,700 93.53 77.51 -81.55 250 37% price ≥ $500 242 854.84 482.29 -852.91 700 122% availability = 0 3,442 47.47 22.25 -18.15 100 47% availability > 0 6,335 64.96 24.43 -31.73 115 56% minimum nights ≥ 30 893 88.66 25.14 -55.44 130 68% minimum nights < 30 8,884 55.80 23.49 -24.08 101 55%

Patterns and our hypothesis for each:

  1. The error follows the price, and the model is pulled towards the middle. Listings below $50 are overestimated by $19.56 on average, listings between $200 and $500 are underestimated by $81.55, and listings above $500 by $852.91. Hypothesis: the features do not contain what makes a listing expensive within its cell (size, number of bedrooms, finish, view are not in the file), so the network predicts something close to the median of listings that look the same, and the extremes on both sides are pulled to it. Predicting on the log scale makes this worse on the expensive side, since expm1 of a mean log is a median, which is below the mean of a right-skewed distribution.
  2. Manhattan and entire homes have the largest errors in dollars, $82.35 and \(84.32, but relative to their median price they are not far from the rest (55% and 53%). *Hypothesis:* they are the most expensive cells and also the ones with the widest spread of prices (EDA Figure 10), so the same relative error is more dollars. The worst neighbourhoods with at least 30 test listings are Greenwich Village (\)198.50), West Village (\(160.37) and SoHo (\)142.88), all in the expensive core where townhouses sit next to studios; the best are Ridgewood (\(18.83), Sunnyside (\)19.11) and Jackson Heights ($19.60).
  3. Listings with minimum nights ≥ 30 have a MAE of $88.66 vs $55.80. Hypothesis: these are the monthly rentals the EDA found at the 30-night spike (EDA Figure 4a), and some hosts type a monthly price in the nightly field. The two worst examples below with 30+ nights are exactly that.
  4. Closed calendars are easier, not harder. The EDA flagged availability_365 == 0 as a risk (stale prices); the MAE there is $47.47 against $64.96 for open calendars. Hypothesis: closed listings are cheaper (median $100 vs $115), and the absurd prices are mostly on open calendars (8 of the 10 worst examples below), probably hosts who are still active and experimenting with the price.
  5. Staten Island has the largest relative error (58%) with only 78 test listings and 295 training listings in the EDA. Hypothesis: too few examples to learn its price level; the network leans on what it learned from Brooklyn and Queens.

The 10 worst predictions:

price ($) predicted ($) error ($) neighbourhood room min nights reviews availability title 9,999 117 9,882 East Harlem Entire home 5 1 0 "Spanish Harlem Apt" 10,000 177 9,823 Upper West Side Entire home 30 0 83 "1-BR Lincoln Center" 7,500 65 7,435 East Flatbush Private room 1 8 179 "Gem of east Flatbush" 7,703 379 7,324 Upper East Side Entire home 1 0 146 "East 72nd Townhouse by (Hidden by Airbnb)" 6,000 243 5,757 Greenwich Village Entire home 1 0 0 "Luxury townhouse Greenwich Village" 4,200 62 4,138 Bedford-Stuyvesant Private room 114 0 347 "Beautiful private Brooklyn room with kitchenette" 3,900 165 3,735 Greenwich Village Entire home 30 7 180 "Greenwich Village Townhome with Private Garden!" 4,000 280 3,720 West Village Entire home 1 0 173 "The Otheroom Bar/Event/Filming Space -read details" 3,600 215 3,385 Upper East Side Entire home 31 0 358 "NYC HOLIDAY!!!! April 15- May 15" 3,613 598 3,015 Upper West Side Entire home 1 1 158 "West 84th Street by (Hidden by Airbnb)"

They fall into four groups, and none of them is fixed by a bigger network:

  • Placeholder prices ($9,999 for a Spanish Harlem apartment with a closed calendar, $7,500 for a private room in East Flatbush). Nobody pays this; the host set the price to block bookings. The network's $117 and $65 are probably closer to what these places are worth.
  • Monthly prices in the nightly field ($10,000 at 30 nights, $4,200 for a private room at 114 nights, $3,600 for "April 15 - May 15"). The minimum-nights column tells part of the story, which is why that group has a high error.
  • Real luxury listings (the two townhouses, the "(Hidden by Airbnb)" listings from a 12-listing host). The price is real, but nothing in the features says "townhouse"; the title does.
  • Not lodging at all ("Bar/Event/Filming Space").

docs.title: Permutation importance
docs.text:
For each of the 10 original columns we shuffled its values across the test rows (5 times, seed 42), passed the shuffled table through the fitted pipeline and measured how much the test MAE went up. Shuffling the raw column, before the pipeline, means neighbourhood and its 104 dummies count as one feature. Because the four location columns carry overlapping information, we also shuffled them together.

column MLP: MAE increase ($) Ridge: MAE increase ($) room_type 25.98 ± 0.49 25.57 ± 0.40 all location together (lat, long, borough, neighbourhood) 17.46 ± 0.41 14.87 ± 0.41 availability_365 6.65 ± 0.33 3.98 ± 0.15 minimum_nights 6.33 ± 0.18 2.44 ± 0.10 longitude 6.20 ± 0.19 1.63 ± 0.09 calculated_host_listings_count 4.99 ± 0.36 0.10 ± 0.01 neighbourhood 4.36 ± 0.07 5.11 ± 0.13 number_of_reviews 3.73 ± 0.13 0.98 ± 0.06 neighbourhood_group 3.05 ± 0.13 7.23 ± 0.18 latitude 2.48 ± 0.16 0.01 ± 0.02 reviews_per_month 1.86 ± 0.14 -0.01 ± 0.01

Does it match the EDA? Mostly yes, with one surprise.

  • Room type first, location second. The EDA said room type is the strongest single predictor (entire homes at 2.3× a private room, Figure 10) and location the second (borough and neighbourhood raised the explained variance from 45.4% to 53.7%). Here room type costs $26 when shuffled and location as a block $17.5, far ahead of everything else, for both models.
  • Latitude and longitude need a nonlinear model. The EDA argued that price depends on distance to lower Manhattan, a 2-D shape a linear model on each coordinate cannot draw (Figure 9). Ridge barely uses the coordinates ($1.63 and \(0.01) and relies on the borough dummies (\)7.23); the network does the opposite, $6.20 + $2.48 on the coordinates and $3.05 on the borough. This is the clearest sign that the network learned something the linear model did not.
  • The surprise: the "how the listing is operated" features matter. The EDA found weak rank correlations between price and availability, minimum nights or host portfolio size (all below 0.11 in absolute value) and PCA showed those features carry little price gradient. For the network they are the next most important after room type and location ($6.65, $6.33, \(4.99), and much more than for Ridge (\)0.10 for host listings). They act through interactions (a 30-night minimum means something different in Manhattan and in the Bronx, a host with 50 listings prices differently from a single-listing host), which a correlation with the target cannot see.
  • The redundant pair. reviews_per_month is the least important column for both models, consistent with the EDA's finding that it overlaps with number_of_reviews (Spearman 0.71). It is the first column we would drop.

docs.title: 7. Conclusion
docs.text:
Was the network worth it? As a model of this table, only partly. It beats the linear baseline by 4.95% on the test MAE, a gap 13.6 times the variation between seeds, and permutation importance shows where the gain comes from: the 2-D geography and the interactions with how the listing is operated. But it missed the 10% we set as the criterion, and gradient boosting with default settings matches it ($58.71 vs $59.10) in a fraction of the time and with no tuning. If the goal were only the lowest MAE on this dataset, we would ship the boosting model. The network was worth it as a check: it says that most of what can be learned from these 10 columns is already learned by either nonlinear model, and that the remaining error is in the data, not in the model.

Limitations.

  • The features cannot see size or quality. Section 6 shows the largest errors are real luxury listings or prices that are not nightly prices, and nothing in the 10 columns separates them from ordinary listings.
  • The target itself is noisy: placeholder prices and monthly prices are in the training set too, and the network learns from them (Huber limits how much).
  • The split is random by listing, as the course asks, but one host can own up to 327 listings with a shared pricing policy (EDA section 5). A split grouped by host_id would probably give a higher test error.
  • It is a mid-2019 snapshot. Prices have changed since, and New York's 2023 short-term rental rules removed a large part of these listings from the market. The model should not be used on today's prices.
  • The hyperparameter ranking is within seed noise (section 4); the chosen configuration is one of several equivalent ones.

Who would be affected by an error. A host who used the model to set a price would be pushed towards the median of similar listings. For a cheap listing (under $50) the model overestimates by $19.56 on average, so a host in the Bronx or Queens following it would price above the market and lose bookings, and that is the group with the least room for a loss. For an expensive listing the model underestimates by hundreds of dollars, so the owner would leave money on the table. If a platform used it to flag "overpriced" listings, the flags would fall on the expensive end of Manhattan, where the error is largest. Any use like this should come with a range, not a single number.

With more time we would: (1) clean the target, removing or flagging placeholder prices and dividing monthly prices by 30; (2) add features from the name column ("townhouse", "month", "event space") with a small text encoder; (3) try a learned embedding for neighbourhood instead of one-hot; (4) train with a quantile (pinball) loss at 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 to give a host a price range; (5) evaluate with a split grouped by host; (6) average the 5 seeds into one ensemble, which costs nothing at this size.
